subtopic_detail: Unilateral absent red reflex found at the six week check in an infant with no ocular discharge or watering
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing the six week check on a boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother says that in photographs taken over the last fortnight the middle of his left eye looks cloudy and pale, and that he does not seem to look at her with that eye.

His eyes are not sticky and do not water. The newborn examination on day one recorded red reflexes present and symmetrical. He is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile, and there is no family history of childhood eye disease.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex absent on the left and present on the right, left pupil appears grey-white to the direct ophthalmoscope, no conjunctival injection or discharge, corneal diameters equal, eyes of equal size
data_table.Visual behaviour: Fixes and follows the examiner's face steadily when the left eye is covered, becomes distressed and turns away when the right eye is covered

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Repeat the red reflex examination at the four month health check
options.rationale: Deferring re-examination wastes the window in which occlusion amblyopia becomes irreversible, and an absent red reflex is never a finding to observe. The mother's account of a change since the newborn check makes progression rather than resolution the expectation. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.text: Refer to a community optometrist for refraction within three months
options.rationale: Refraction assesses focusing error in an eye with a clear media and does not address an opacity blocking the reflex. The near pair here is that optometric refraction is the right pathway for a squint with an intact red reflex, which is not this child. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.text: Arrange paediatric ophthalmology assessment within the next week
options.rationale: An absent red reflex in one eye requires ophthalmological assessment within days, both because a media opacity must be cleared early enough to allow the visual pathway to develop and because an intraocular tumour presents this way. Deprivation from a dense unilateral opacity produces dense amblyopia if the eye is not treated in the first months of life. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.text: Request TORCH serology and review the infant when results return
options.rationale: Congenital infection is one cause of a media opacity but serology takes days and does not change the immediate need for specialist examination. Investigating aetiology before securing the eye assessment inverts the order of priorities. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cataract)

options.text: Order a cranial ultrasound and review once the scan is reported
options.rationale: Cranial ultrasound images the brain and does not resolve the anterior segment or the retina to the standard needed here. A normal scan would falsely reassure while the visual deprivation continues. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cataract)

explanation.summary: The red reflex is the single most useful screening test of the paediatric eye in primary care, and it is performed at the newborn check, the six to eight week check and whenever a parent reports an abnormal appearance. An absent, dull or asymmetric reflex means light is not returning from the retina, which places a media opacity, a retinal detachment or an intraocular mass in the differential. The visual cortex is plastic only for the first months of life, so a dense unilateral opacity that is not cleared early leaves permanent amblyopia even if the opacity is later removed. Parental reports of an abnormal appearance in photographs are a genuinely useful history, because the camera flash reproduces the test under conditions the parent sees repeatedly.
key_points: An absent red reflex is a referral finding in its own right, not an observation finding
A normal newborn red reflex does not exclude an opacity developing later in infancy
Absent discharge and watering argue against nasolacrimal duct obstruction as the cause
Objection to occlusion of one eye implies the fellow eye is the seeing eye
Aetiological investigation must not delay the specialist eye assessment
explanation.pearls: Surgery for a dense unilateral congenital cataract gives the best visual outcome when performed between four and six weeks of age, which is why an absent red reflex found at the six week check is a same week referral rather than a routine one.

sources.label: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Angle of trunk rotation of eight degrees on forward bending in a thirteen year old girl eleven months after menarche
stem:
A 13 year old girl is brought to your general practice because her mother noticed that one shoulder sits higher than the other and that one side of her back sticks up when she bends forward to pick things up. She has no back pain, no night pain and no change in bowel or bladder function.

Her menarche was eleven months ago. On examination she is well grown, her skin shows no birthmarks or patches of altered pigmentation, her foot arches are normal on standing and reflexes are symmetrical with downgoing plantar responses. On the Adams forward bend test there is a right thoracic prominence, and a scoliometer placed over it reads 8 degrees.

data_table.Examination: Right thoracic rib prominence on forward bending with a scoliometer angle of trunk rotation of 8 degrees, shoulder heights unequal by approximately 2 cm, waist creases asymmetric, no midline skin lesion over the spine, no cafe au lait macules, normal pes planus free foot arches, power and reflexes normal and symmetrical in both legs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure and review her in twelve months with a repeat examination
options.rationale: A twelve month interval is far too long in a girl less than two years past menarche, when the residual growth spurt drives the majority of curve progression. Observation without a baseline radiograph also leaves the curve magnitude unknown. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Arrange a standing whole spine radiograph and refer to a spine clinic
options.rationale: A scoliometer angle of trunk rotation at or above 7 degrees is the accepted threshold for imaging, because it corresponds to a curve likely to be clinically significant, and management decisions depend on the Cobb angle measured on an erect film. Referral alongside imaging allows skeletal maturity and curve magnitude to be combined into a progression risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine before review
options.rationale: Spinal magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for features suggesting an underlying neural axis abnormality, such as a left thoracic curve, a midline skin lesion, a cavus foot, asymmetric reflexes or pain waking the child. None of those features is present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a scoliosis specific exercise programme
options.rationale: Scoliosis specific exercises are an adjunct considered once a curve has been measured and staged, not a substitute for establishing the Cobb angle. Starting therapy without imaging risks missing a curve already in the bracing or surgical range. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

options.text: Fit a thoracolumbosacral brace and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Bracing is indicated for a curve between about 25 and 40 degrees in a patient with remaining growth, so it cannot be prescribed before the Cobb angle is known. Bracing an unmeasured curve exposes the patient to a demanding treatment that may be unnecessary. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a structural three dimensional deformity that produces rotation as well as lateral curvature, which is why the rib prominence on forward bending is the physical sign rather than the visible curve itself. Risk of progression is driven by the curve magnitude and the growth remaining, so skeletal maturity markers such as time since menarche and the Risser sign are as important as the Cobb angle. Curves under 25 degrees are usually observed, curves between about 25 and 40 degrees in a growing patient are braced, and curves beyond about 45 to 50 degrees are considered for surgery. Features pointing away from idiopathic disease include pain, a left thoracic curve, neurological signs and cutaneous markers, each of which redirects the workup towards imaging of the neural axis.
key_points: The scoliometer measures trunk rotation, and 7 degrees is the usual threshold for radiography
Progression risk is highest in the two years spanning the pubertal growth spurt
Management is decided on the Cobb angle from an erect whole spine film
Normal reflexes, normal foot arches and no skin lesions argue against a neural axis cause
A right thoracic curve is the expected pattern in idiopathic disease
explanation.pearls: A left sided thoracic curve in an adolescent is atypical for idiopathic scoliosis and should prompt magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine to look for a syrinx, a Chiari malformation or a cord tumour, even when the neurological examination is normal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs with a raised alkaline phosphatase in an eighteen month old who is still breastfed and has had very little sun exposure
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl referred because her legs have become increasingly bowed since she started walking at 14 months. Her mother describes her as slow to get going in the mornings and says she does not like to walk far.

She is still breastfed with small amounts of family food and has never taken a vitamin supplement. The family covers up outdoors for cultural reasons and the child spends almost all of her time inside. Her length is on the 10th centile having previously tracked the 50th, and her weight is on the 25th centile. There is widening of both wrists on palpation and a symmetrical outward bowing of both tibiae.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum with an intercondylar distance of 6 cm, palpable widening of both distal radial metaphyses, prominence of the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, no joint swelling or tenderness, normal muscle bulk with mildly reduced proximal power
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (1.10 to 1.90), alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (110 to 320), parathyroid hormone markedly elevated, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (greater than 50), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral calcium carbonate alone for three months with no vitamin supplement
options.rationale: Calcium alone does not correct the substrate deficiency driving the secondary hyperparathyroidism, so the bone disease persists and the parathyroid hormone stays elevated. Calcium deficiency rickets with a normal vitamin D level is the situation in which calcium alone is appropriate. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.text: Oral calcitriol 0.25 micrograms daily for three months plus dietary calcium
options.rationale: Calcitriol bypasses renal hydroxylation and is reserved for renal disease or the rare hydroxylase defects, neither of which fits normal renal function with a profoundly low 25 hydroxyvitamin D. Its narrow therapeutic index makes hypercalcaemia a real hazard in nutritional deficiency. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.text: Oral cholecalciferol 400 units daily for three months plus dietary calcium
options.rationale: Four hundred units is the daily dose used to prevent deficiency in an at risk infant, not to heal established rickets, and at this dose the radiological and biochemical abnormalities correct slowly if at all. The near pair here is prevention dosing against treatment dosing of the same drug. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.text: No supplement for three months with repeat biochemistry and a bone survey
options.rationale: Untreated rickets continues to deform the growing skeleton and carries a risk of hypocalcaemic seizures and cardiomyopathy in young children. A skeletal survey adds radiation without altering the treatment that the biochemistry already indicates. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Oral cholecalciferol 3000 units daily for three months plus dietary calcium
options.rationale: Established nutritional rickets in a child over twelve months is treated with high dose cholecalciferol for three months, together with an adequate calcium intake because healing bone consumes calcium rapidly. Treatment dosing is an order of magnitude above prevention dosing, and maintenance supplementation continues once the course is complete. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains common in Australian children whose skin is rarely exposed to sunlight, whether because of latitude, clothing practices, or prolonged indoor time, and exclusive or prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation compounds the risk because breast milk contains very little vitamin D. The biochemical signature is a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with a raised alkaline phosphatase and a raised parathyroid hormone, with phosphate falling as parathyroid hormone drives renal phosphate loss and calcium held near the lower limit until decompensation. Normal renal function distinguishes nutritional disease from the rickets of chronic kidney disease, and a raised parathyroid hormone distinguishes it from X linked hypophosphataemia, where parathyroid hormone is normal or only slightly raised. Radiographs of the wrist show cupping, splaying and fraying of the metaphysis and are useful for confirming healing.
key_points: Alkaline phosphatase is the most sensitive routine marker of active rickets in a child
Secondary hyperparathyroidism explains the low phosphate and the near normal calcium
Normal renal function excludes renal osteodystrophy as the explanation
Treatment dosing of cholecalciferol is far higher than prevention dosing
Calcium intake must be adequate during healing or hypocalcaemia can worsen
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase rises further in the first weeks of vitamin D treatment as the bone heals before it falls, so a rising value at the four week review is evidence of response rather than treatment failure.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents
Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Purulent conjunctivitis beginning on day nine of life with a negative gonococcal culture and a positive chlamydial nucleic acid test
stem:
You are the resident in the emergency department reviewing a nine day old boy whose mother says his eyes have been gluey and his eyelids puffy for three days, and that the discharge keeps coming back after she wipes it away. He was born at term at home, and his mother booked late in the pregnancy and had no antenatal screening swabs taken.

He is afebrile, feeding well and has gained weight since discharge. Both conjunctivae are injected with a copious yellow discharge and marked lid oedema, and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining. A conjunctival swab shows no organisms on Gram stain and culture is negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, while nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral lid oedema with copious mucopurulent discharge, conjunctival injection without follicles, clear corneas on fluorescein staining, chest clear on auscultation with no cough, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Conjunctival swab Gram stain shows polymorphs with no organisms seen, culture negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol ointment and review of the mother and her partner
options.rationale: Chloramphenicol has poor activity against this organism and topical therapy alone does not reach the nasopharyngeal reservoir, so up to a fifth of infants go on to develop a pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks. Chloramphenicol is a reasonable choice for ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis beyond the neonatal period. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral azithromycin for the infant and treatment of the mother and her partner
options.rationale: Systemic therapy is required because the organism colonises the nasopharynx as well as the conjunctiva, and oral azithromycin for the infant is the Australian regimen of choice. The infection is sexually transmitted, so the mother and her sexual partners must be treated and offered testing for other infections at the same time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone for the infant and treatment of mother and partner
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is the treatment for gonococcal ophthalmia, which is excluded here by a negative Gram stain and culture, and it has no useful activity against this organism. Ceftriaxone also displaces bilirubin from albumin, which is an added reason to avoid it in the neonate without indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical erythromycin ointment and treatment of the mother and her partner
options.rationale: Erythromycin has the right spectrum but the wrong route, since topical delivery clears the eye while leaving the nasopharynx colonised and the pneumonitis risk untouched. The near pair here is that the same drug class given systemically would be an acceptable alternative regimen. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Saline eye toilet alone and review of the mother and her partner in a week
options.rationale: Eye toilet is useful supportive care but does not eradicate an organism that causes scarring conjunctivitis and later respiratory disease if untreated. Saline alone is appropriate for the sticky eye of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, where there is watering without lid oedema or purulent discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset and by the organism, because the treatment and the consequences differ sharply. Gonococcal disease presents within the first two to five days with hyperacute purulent discharge and threatens the cornea within hours, whereas chlamydial disease presents at the end of the first week to the middle of the second with a more indolent mucopurulent discharge and lid swelling. Chlamydial infection is acquired during passage through the birth canal and colonises the nasopharynx as well as the eye, which is why systemic rather than topical therapy is mandatory and why an afebrile infant with a staccato cough at six weeks may be the same infection presenting again. Any neonatal chlamydial or gonococcal infection is a sexually transmitted infection in the mother, so contact tracing and testing for co-infection are part of the management, not an optional extra.
key_points: Onset at the end of the first week points away from gonococcal disease
A negative Gram stain and culture for Neisseria excludes the hyperacute sight threatening cause
Topical therapy leaves the nasopharyngeal reservoir and the pneumonitis risk untreated
Maternal and partner treatment with contact tracing is part of the infant's management
Clear corneas on fluorescein staining exclude established corneal involvement
explanation.pearls: Chlamydial pneumonitis appears between four and twelve weeks of age as an afebrile infant with a staccato cough, tachypnoea and eosinophilia, and a history of a sticky eye in the second week of life is often the only clue linking the two presentations.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear in a four year old with a temperature of 38.7 degrees and a C reactive protein of 62
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 4 year old boy who has refused to stand since waking this morning and cries when his mother lifts him. He had a mild runny nose a week ago that has since settled, and there has been no injury.

He looks unwell and flushed. He lies with the right hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and he resists any passive movement through more than about 10 degrees in any direction. There is no rash, no joint swelling elsewhere and no bony tenderness over the tibia or femoral shaft.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed abducted and externally rotated with guarding through a 10 degree arc, no effusion palpable at the knee, no overlying erythema or warmth over the thigh, no rash, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h (less than 15), blood culture collected, hip radiograph shows no fracture and no femoral head abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for hip joint aspiration under anaesthesia
options.rationale: He meets four of the predictors used to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis, which places the probability of infection high enough that the joint must be sampled. Aspiration under anaesthesia confirms the diagnosis and decompresses a joint whose cartilage and femoral head blood supply are at risk within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

options.text: Oral ibuprofen and review in forty eight hours if he is not improving
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory treatment and review is the pathway for transient synovitis, which typically follows a viral illness in a child who is afebrile, still weight bears with a limp and has normal or near normal inflammatory markers. A temperature of 38.7 degrees with a C reactive protein of 62 and complete refusal to weight bear does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and review the response overnight
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration reduce the yield of synovial culture and can leave the child on a prolonged empirical course without an organism or a drained joint. Antibiotics are started immediately after the sample is taken, not instead of taking it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a hip radiograph and review once the film has been reported
options.rationale: A radiograph has already been taken and is normal, which is expected because plain films stay normal for the first one to two weeks of joint or bone infection. Repeating imaging that cannot exclude the diagnosis simply delays the definitive test. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

options.text: Arrange bone scintigraphy and review once the scan has been reported
options.rationale: Scintigraphy is a second line study when the site of infection is genuinely unclear, and it takes hours to arrange while adding radiation. Here the hip is clinically localised, so the sampling procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children

explanation.summary: The irritable hip in a young child sits on a spectrum from transient synovitis, which is self limiting, to septic arthritis, which destroys cartilage and can infarct the femoral head within days. The Kocher predictors of fever above 38.5 degrees, refusal to weight bear, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 and a white cell count above 12 stratify that risk, with the probability of infection rising steeply as the number of predictors increases, and Australian practice adds a C reactive protein above 20 as a further strong predictor. Ultrasound reliably shows an effusion but cannot distinguish an infected effusion from a sterile one, so it guides aspiration rather than replacing it. The hip is held flexed, abducted and externally rotated in both conditions because that position maximises capsular volume and minimises intracapsular pressure.
key_points: The position of comfort is common to both diagnoses and does not discriminate
Plain radiographs are normal early in septic arthritis and cannot exclude it
Ultrasound shows an effusion but cannot tell an infected joint from a sterile one
Synovial fluid must be obtained before antibiotics wherever possible
A preceding viral illness is compatible with either diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A child with an irritable hip who is afebrile, weight bears with a limp and has a C reactive protein below 20 can usually be managed as transient synovitis with review in 48 hours, whereas any one of fever above 38.5 degrees, complete refusal to weight bear, or a C reactive protein above 20 moves the child into the aspiration pathway.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children

subtopic_detail: Soiling most days in a six year old with a palpable abdominal faecal mass who passed meconium on the first day of life
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old boy whose parents report that he is dirtying his underpants almost every day and that the smell has become a problem at school. They say he opens his bowels properly only once every week or so, and that when he does the stool is so large it blocks the toilet.

He passed his first bowel motion on the day he was born and grew normally through infancy. He is now withholding, standing on tiptoes and crossing his legs when he feels the urge. His abdomen is soft with a firm indentable mass palpable in the left iliac fossa and suprapubically. The perianal skin is normal, anal tone is normal on inspection with no fissure seen, and the lower limb neurological examination and back are normal.

data_table.Examination: Weight and height tracking the 50th centile, abdomen soft and non tender with a firm indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa extending suprapubically, normally sited anus with normal perianal sensation, no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal power tone and reflexes in both legs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: A phosphate enema daily until the impaction clears, then maintenance
options.rationale: Rectal treatment is distressing in a child who is already withholding and reinforces the aversion that drives the cycle, and repeated phosphate enemas carry a risk of electrolyte disturbance. Enemas are reserved for oral disimpaction that has failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: A lactulose maintenance dose with a high fibre diet and toilet sitting
options.rationale: Starting maintenance without clearing the impaction leaves soft stool to leak past the retained mass, so the soiling continues and the family concludes the treatment has failed. The near pair here is that this is exactly the right regimen once disimpaction is complete. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: An escalating oral macrogol regimen followed by a maintenance dose
options.rationale: The overflow soiling is caused by liquid stool passing around a retained faecal mass, so the mass must be cleared before any maintenance regimen can work, and an escalating oral macrogol course achieves this without rectal intervention. Maintenance then continues for months, because stopping as soon as the stools normalise is the commonest cause of relapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Referral for manual evacuation under anaesthesia, then maintenance
options.rationale: Manual evacuation under anaesthesia is a last resort for impaction resistant to oral and rectal treatment, and it exposes the child to an anaesthetic for a problem that usually resolves medically. It is not a first line intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Referral for anorectal manometry before any laxative is commenced
options.rationale: Manometry and rectal biopsy investigate an aganglionic segment, which is made unlikely by passage of meconium on the first day, normal growth and a rectum loaded with stool rather than empty. Investigating before treating delays relief in a child with a clear functional picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children

explanation.summary: Faecal incontinence in a school aged child is usually overflow from chronic functional constipation rather than a behavioural problem, and framing it that way to the family is an important part of the consultation because blame is common and unhelpful. The cycle starts with a painful or frightening stool, leads to withholding, and produces a dilated rectum that loses the sensation of fullness so that soft stool leaks past the retained mass without the child noticing. Treatment has two distinct phases, disimpaction and then maintenance, and skipping the first phase is the commonest reason treatment appears to fail. Red flags that redirect the workup include delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, ribbon stools with an empty rectum, faltering growth, a sacral dimple or hair tuft, and abnormal lower limb neurology.
key_points: Soiling in this setting is overflow incontinence, not deliberate behaviour
Disimpaction must precede maintenance or the soiling continues
Passage of meconium on day one makes an aganglionic segment unlikely
A normal back and normal lower limb neurology argue against a spinal cause
Maintenance is continued for months, and stopping early causes relapse
explanation.pearls: Warn the family before starting disimpaction that soiling usually gets worse for the first several days as the retained mass breaks up, because families who are not warned stop the macrogol at exactly the point it is starting to work.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children

subtopic_detail: Escherichia coli sepsis with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a nine day old whose urine gives positive reducing substances with a negative glucose oxidase strip
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar looking after a nine day old girl admitted with lethargy and poor feeding who has grown Escherichia coli from her blood culture and is on intravenous antibiotics. Her mother says she fed well for the first few days at home and then became increasingly sleepy and vomited after most feeds once her milk came in properly.

She was born at term at a birth centre and the newborn screening card was collected on day three but the result is not yet available. She is jaundiced to the abdomen and her liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Her urine tests positive for reducing substances while the bedside glucose oxidase strip on the same sample is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 58/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 56 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Lethargic with reduced tone, jaundice extending to the abdomen, liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 268 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 92 micromol/L (conjugated less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 148 U/L (less than 45), albumin 28 g/L (35 to 50), international normalised ratio 1.9 (0.9 to 1.3), blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5), blood culture growing Escherichia coli, urine reducing substances positive with a negative glucose oxidase strip

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her feeding management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and start phototherapy for the raised bilirubin
options.rationale: Phototherapy acts on unconjugated bilirubin and does nothing for a conjugated fraction of 92 micromol/L, and continuing lactose containing milk sustains the toxic metabolite load. A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia always signals liver disease rather than the exaggerated physiological jaundice that phototherapy treats. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Stop lactose containing feeds and change to a soy based formula
options.rationale: Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose oxidase strip means a non glucose reducing sugar is present, which in a jaundiced neonate with coagulopathy and Gram negative sepsis points to galactose accumulation, and the specific treatment is immediate removal of dietary galactose. Waiting for the newborn screening result risks progressive liver failure, so the feed is changed on suspicion and the diagnostic samples are taken alongside. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and start ursodeoxycholic acid for the jaundice
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid is a bile flow agent used in established cholestatic disease and does not address a substrate that is actively injuring the liver while the feed continues. It would leave the galactose load in place. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Galactosaemia)

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and continue the antibiotics
options.rationale: Extensively hydrolysed formulas break down the protein but most still contain lactose, so the offending sugar is delivered unchanged. The near pair here is that the hydrolysed formula is the right answer for cow's milk protein allergy, where the protein rather than the sugar is the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

options.text: Stop all enteral feeds and start intravenous ten per cent dextrose alone
options.rationale: Dextrose corrects the hypoglycaemia but prolonged starvation of a septic neonate is not a sustainable plan, and a galactose free feed both removes the substrate and provides nutrition. Intravenous glucose is a useful adjunct rather than the definitive feeding decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia presents in the first two weeks once milk feeding is established, because galactose from lactose accumulates as galactose 1 phosphate and injures the liver, kidney and brain. The triad that should trigger suspicion is a jaundiced unwell neonate with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, and Gram negative sepsis, since Escherichia coli sepsis is characteristically associated with the condition through impaired neutrophil function. Newborn screening in Australia includes galactosaemia, but the result may not be back before the infant becomes unwell, so the diagnosis is made clinically and the feed is changed immediately rather than waiting. Even with prompt dietary treatment, long term outcomes include learning difficulties and primary ovarian insufficiency in girls, so treatment is not curative and follow up is lifelong.
key_points: Positive reducing substances with a negative glucose strip indicates a non glucose sugar
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a neonate always indicates liver disease
Gram negative sepsis is characteristically associated with this metabolic disorder
Dietary galactose is removed on suspicion rather than after confirmation
Hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy reflect hepatic involvement rather than sepsis alone
explanation.pearls: Galactose free soy formula is started on clinical suspicion, but the diagnostic red cell galactose 1 phosphate uridyltransferase assay must be taken before any red cell transfusion, because transfused donor enzyme masks the deficiency for up to three months.
